lead: A signal constellation draws every waveform a modulator can send as a point in a signal space built from orthonormal basis functions. The distances between the points set the error probability; the number of points sets the bits per symbol and, with the pulse shape, the bandwidth. Put the spectra of the schemes side by side and the picture also shows how much band each one really occupies. Every modem, from a GPS receiver to 1024-QAM Wi-Fi, is designed on these two pictures.
prereq: You need: the schemes of BPSK, M-ary PSK, QAM and MFSK and MSK.

blocks.text: For passband symbols of length T<sub>s</sub>, two orthonormal basis functions carry everything: φ<sub>1</sub>(t) = √(2/T<sub>s</sub>)cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t) and φ<sub>2</sub>(t) = −√(2/T<sub>s</sub>)sin(2πf<sub>c</sub> t). Each has unit energy and their product integrates to zero over a symbol. A symbol s<sub>i</sub>(t) = s<sub>i1</sub>φ<sub>1</sub>(t) + s<sub>i2</sub>φ<sub>2</sub>(t) is the point (s<sub>i1</sub>, s<sub>i2</sub>), with energy E<sub>i</sub> = s<sub>i1</sub>² + s<sub>i2</sub>²; the average over M equally likely symbols is E<sub>s</sub>.

The receiver correlates with φ<sub>1</sub> and φ<sub>2</sub>, gets a noisy point, and picks the nearest constellation point. The set of points nearer to s<sub>i</sub> than to any other is its decision region.

d<sub>min</sub> is the smallest distance between two points, N<sub>nb</sub> the number of nearest neighbours of a point and N<sub>0</sub>/2 the two-sided noise density. A symbol is lost when noise pushes it across a boundary d<sub>min</sub>/2 away.

16-QAM with levels ±a, ±3a has E<sub>s</sub> = 10a² and d<sub>min</sub> = 2a, so d<sub>min</sub>² = 0.4E<sub>s</sub> = 1.6E<sub>b</sub>. At the same E<sub>b</sub> it keeps its points much further apart than 16-PSK, which is why large constellations use QAM grids, not circles.

sections.h3: Size sets the bits and the bandwidth

blocks.text: M points carry k = log<sub>2</sub> M bits, so R<sub>b</sub> = kR<sub>s</sub>. The bandwidth efficiency η = R<sub>b</sub>/B is measured in b/s/Hz, never in bits per symbol. With rectangular pulses the passband main lobe is B = 2R<sub>s</sub> wide, so η = k/2; with ideal Nyquist pulses B = R<sub>s</sub> and η = k. Orthogonal MFSK needs about M·R<sub>s</sub>/2, so η = 2k/M falls as M grows.

On a plane of η across and required E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> up, PSK and QAM move right and up as M grows (more bits per hertz, more power per bit), MFSK moves left and down. The Shannon limit bounds the plane: η ≤ log<sub>2</sub>(1 + SNR), or per bit E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> ≥ (2<sup>η</sup> − 1)/η, which tends to −1.59 dB as η → 0. Coding (see information theory and error-control coding) is what closes the gap.

f is measured from the carrier and sinc x = sin(πx)/(πx). The passband spectrum is this shape centred on ±f<sub>c</sub>.

QPSK has the narrowest main lobe, but MSK puts almost all its power in a tight band, so it disturbs neighbouring channels far less. That is why constant-envelope MSK and GMSK were chosen for crowded mobile bands.

examples.question: A 10 MHz passband channel takes rectangular-pulse signals whose null-to-null band is 2R<sub>s</sub>. Find the symbol rate and the bit rate and efficiency for BPSK, QPSK and 16-QAM, and say how much more E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> 16-QAM needs for the same error rate.
steps: R<sub>s</sub> = B/2 = 5 Msymbol/s for all three.
BPSK: k = 1, R<sub>b</sub> = 5 Mb/s, η = 0.5 b/s/Hz.
QPSK: k = 2, R<sub>b</sub> = 10 Mb/s, η = 1 b/s/Hz.

Power: d<sub>min</sub>² is 4E<sub>b</sub> for BPSK and QPSK but 1.6E<sub>b</sub> for 16-QAM; 10 log<sub>10</sub>(4/1.6) = 10 log<sub>10</sub> 2.5 = 3.98 dB, about 4 dB more (a little more again because a 16-QAM point has more neighbours).
examples.answer: R<sub>s</sub> = 5 Msymbol/s; 5, 10 and 20 Mb/s at 0.5, 1 and 2 b/s/Hz; 16-QAM needs about 4 dB more E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>.

examples.question: Compare BPSK, QPSK and MSK at R<sub>b</sub> = 10 kb/s: main-lobe width, 99% bandwidth, and the side-lobe level 2.5R<sub>b</sub> from the carrier relative to the BPSK peak.
steps: Main lobes: BPSK 2R<sub>b</sub> = 20 kHz; QPSK R<sub>b</sub> = 10 kHz; MSK 1.5R<sub>b</sub> = 15 kHz.
99% bands: BPSK 20.6 × 10 = 206 kHz; QPSK 103 kHz; MSK 1.2 × 10 = 12 kHz.
At fT<sub>b</sub> = 2.5: BPSK 2E<sub>b</sub>·sinc²(2.5) = 2E<sub>b</sub> × 0.0162, which is −17.9 dB from its peak 2E<sub>b</sub>.
MSK: (32/π²)[cos 5π/(100 − 1)]² E<sub>b</sub> = 3.242 × 1.02 × 10<sup>−4</sup> E<sub>b</sub> = 3.31 × 10<sup>−4</sup> E<sub>b</sub>, which is −37.8 dB from 2E<sub>b</sub>.
Check: MSK is 20 dB quieter there although its main lobe is half as wide again as QPSK's.
examples.answer: Main lobes 20, 10 and 15 kHz; 99% bands about 206, 103 and 12 kHz; at 2.5R<sub>b</sub> BPSK is −17.9 dB and MSK −37.8 dB relative to the BPSK peak.

traps: η is in b/s/Hz, not bits per symbol: QPSK carries 2 bits per symbol but η = 1 b/s/Hz with rectangular pulses.
Do not use the baseband Nyquist width R<sub>s</sub>/2 for a passband channel; the passband minimum is R<sub>s</sub>.

Compare schemes at the same E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>. At the same E<sub>s</sub>, 16-QAM has half the E<sub>b</sub> of QPSK (E<sub>s</sub> = 4E<sub>b</sub> against 2E<sub>b</sub>), 3 dB less per bit; the 6 dB figure is the comparison with BPSK.
The Q-function takes d<sub>min</sub>/√(2N<sub>0</sub>), a distance; tables often list d<sub>min</sub>², so take the square root first.
QPSK's main lobe is narrower than MSK's, but MSK has far less power outside it; quote both facts in a spectrum comparison.

quiz.q: Define d<sub>min</sub> and E<sub>s</sub> for an M-point constellation.
quiz.a: d<sub>min</sub> is the smallest distance between any two points; E<sub>s</sub> = (1/M)Σ(s<sub>i1</sub>² + s<sub>i2</sub>²).

quiz.q: Give the null-to-null main lobes of BPSK, QPSK and MSK at bit rate R<sub>b</sub>.
Why does raising M at fixed E<sub>s</sub> raise the error rate?
quiz.a: More points share the same energy, so d<sub>min</sub> shrinks and the argument of Q falls.

quiz.q: A 200 kHz channel carries 64-QAM with B = 2R<sub>s</sub>. Find R<sub>s</sub>, R<sub>b</sub> and η.
quiz.a: R<sub>s</sub> = 100 ksymbol/s, R<sub>b</sub> = 600 kb/s, η = 3 b/s/Hz.

quiz.q: How much more E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> does 64-QAM need than BPSK, from d<sub>min</sub>²?
BPSK and QPSK have the same d<sub>min</sub>² = 4E<sub>b</sub>, yet QPSK doubles η. Where do the extra bits come from?
quiz.a: QPSK uses the second basis function, the quadrature carrier, so two antipodal bits share one symbol interval without disturbing each other.

quiz.q: Why did mobile systems pick MSK-type signals although QPSK has the narrower main lobe?
quiz.a: MSK's side lobes start 23 dB down and fall as 1/f⁴, so 99% of its power lies in about 1.2R<sub>b</sub> against about 10R<sub>b</sub> for QPSK; with a constant envelope it also suits efficient amplifiers.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real standards switch constellations while the link runs (adaptive modulation and coding). The last decibels to the Shannon limit are now chased with constellation shaping: geometric shaping moves the points, probabilistic shaping uses the inner points more often, as in modern optical transceivers. Search next: probabilistic constellation shaping, spectral masks, adjacent-channel leakage.

QPSK has the narrowest main lobe (first null at 0.5R<sub>b</sub>, so R<sub>b</sub> null to null), MSK’s first null is at 0.75R<sub>b</sub>, BPSK’s at R<sub>b</sub>; but MSK’s side lobes are far lower, 37.8 dB down at 2.5R<sub>b</sub> against 17.9 dB for BPSK (second worked example).

spec.aria: Three curves in decibels from 5 to minus 50 against frequency offset from 0 to 3 bit rates: BPSK and QPSK sinc-squared curves with side lobes near minus 13 to minus 20 dB, and the MSK curve with a wider main lobe whose side lobes fall much faster. Points at 2.5 bit rates mark minus 17.9 dB for BPSK and minus 37.8 dB for MSK.
